result: The NIR-III laser (1650 nm) demonstrates superior photothermal conversion efficiency compared to NIR-I and NIR-II lasers. The 1.5 W cm⁻² NIR-III laser caused ~40°C temperature increase in aqueous solution within 10 min, and chicken breast surface temperature increased from 27.2°C to 76.7°C. Temperature difference remained >10°C even through 10 mm chicken breast thickness. In contrast, NIR-I (808 nm) showed negligible temperature changes with power adjustment, and NIR-II (980, 1064 nm) showed maximum temperature differences <15°C.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 and C50-C51 provide converging experimental evidence from multiple tissue models (aqueous solution, chicken breast) demonstrating NIR-III's superior photothermal performance. The comparative data with NIR-I and NIR-II lasers (Figures 2c-d, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-3) clearly establish the advantage of NIR-III. The tissue penetration data (C21) further validates practical applicability.

result: NIR-III laser demonstrates consistent tissue penetration capability across different biological tissue types. Temperature ranges of 36.6–91.1°C were achieved in pig fat penetration experiments varying with laser power and fat thickness. Similar attenuation of photothermal efficiency was observed regardless of whether the tissue was chicken breast or pig fat.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by experimental data from multiple tissue models (Figure 3). The consistency across different tissue types (chicken breast and pig fat) strengthens the generalizability of the findings. However, the manuscript would benefit from more detailed statistical analysis of the comparative attenuation rates.

result: NIR-III laser treatment effectively kills MPNST cells in vitro in a power density- and time-dependent manner. In STS26T cells, 0.25 W cm⁻² for 5 min induced 25% cell death, while higher power densities showed strong killing effects. At 10 min, maximum cell death occurred regardless of power density. The NIR-III laser (1 W cm⁻²) achieved almost 100% cell killing efficiency after penetrating 4 mm chicken skin. Flow cytometry confirmed nearly 100% late apoptotic/dead cell populations in multiple treatment conditions.
evaluation: Claims C22-C25, C54-C55 are well-supported by multiple complementary assays (CCK-8, calcein-AM/PI staining, flow cytometry) shown in Figure 4. The dose-response relationship is clearly demonstrated across both cell lines (STS26T and S462). The tissue penetration experiments (C24, C54) provide clinically relevant context. The convergence of multiple independent assays strengthens confidence in the results.

result: NIR-III laser achieves effective photothermal ablation of MPNST xenograft tumors in vivo with power density-dependent penetration depth. In STS26T xenografts, tumor temperature increased from 32.9°C to 60.2°C (0.5 W cm⁻²) and to 75.4°C (1 W cm⁻²) within 10 min. Effective ablation was achieved at 4.5 mm depth with 0.5 W cm⁻² for 10 min, and >7.5 mm depth with 1 W cm⁻² for 10 min, as confirmed by H&E, Ki-67, and Cleaved-Caspase 3 staining.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28, C56 are strongly supported by in vivo temperature measurements (Figure 5a-d) and histological analysis at multiple tissue depths (Figure 5f-h). The use of multiple complementary staining methods (H&E, Ki-67, Cleaved-Caspase 3) provides robust validation. The depth-dependent efficacy is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls.

result: NIR-III laser treatment at 1 W cm⁻² for 5 min completely eradicates STS26T tumors with minimal toxicity, while 0.5 W cm⁻² for 5 min shows incomplete efficacy. Four of seven mice in the lower power group had tumor recurrence after 15 days, while tumors in the higher power group were completely eradicated. More necrotic regions and obvious apoptosis were observed in the 1 W cm⁻² group. No significant pathological toxicity was observed in major organs, and mice showed negligible weight fluctuations.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31, C57-C59 are supported by long-term in vivo efficacy data (Figure 6) including tumor growth curves, survival analysis, histology (H&E, TUNEL), and safety assessment. The comparison between two power densities clearly demonstrates the importance of treatment parameters. The safety data from major organ histology and body weight monitoring (Figure 6f, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) adequately support the biosafety claims.

result: NIR-III treatment induces ER stress response in STS26T tumors, characterized by enrichment of protein processing in ER pathway (hsa04141) and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis pathway (hsa04120). Key UPR transcription factors ATF4 and ATF6B, and ER chaperones P4HB and HSPA1A were significantly upregulated, as confirmed by both RNA-seq and RT-qPCR.
evaluation: Claims C32-C37, C60-C61 are supported by comprehensive transcriptomic analysis (RNA-seq) with appropriate bioinformatics (KEGG, GO enrichment) and independent validation by RT-qPCR (Figure 7). The mechanistic interpretation linking NIR-III treatment to ER stress through pathway analysis is logical and well-supported. However, the RNA-seq appears to use n=1 per group, which is a significant limitation for transcriptomic studies.

result: Different MPNST cell types show heterogeneous responses to NIR-III laser treatment. The ER pathway was not enriched in S462 cells after NIR-III treatment, unlike STS26T cells. STS26T cells exhibited stronger resistance to NIR-III laser treatment than S462 cells, as demonstrated by flow cytometry.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C65 are supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and flow cytometry data (Figure 7—figure supplement 3). The observation of cell line-specific responses is important for understanding treatment variability. However, the mechanistic basis for this heterogeneity requires further investigation beyond the current data.

result: The ER stress response (ERSR) enabled a proportion of STS26T cells to survive NIR-III laser treatment through improving protein-folding capacity and ubiquitylating unfolded proteins. STS26T MPNST cells strongly enhanced the protein processing capacity of the ER to survive the ER stress induced by NIR-III laser treatment.
evaluation: Claims C40 and C71 are explicitly labeled as speculation in the evidence. While the RNA-seq data showing upregulation of ER stress response genes provides circumstantial support, direct functional validation (e.g., using ER stress inhibitors, genetic manipulation of UPR components) is lacking. The causal relationship between ERSR activation and cell survival remains to be experimentally demonstrated.

result: The combination of NIR-III laser treatment with an ER stress inhibitor (such as icariin or ghrelin) could potentially increase therapeutic effectiveness.
evaluation: Claim C41 is explicitly labeled as speculation and represents a proposed future direction rather than a demonstrated result. While the hypothesis is logical based on the ER stress findings, no experimental data testing this combination approach is provided. This requires future validation studies.

result: Despite individual differences in molecular response and treatment efficiency (possibly influenced by different ER stress responses), optimal antineoplastic effects can be achieved by adjusting NIR-III laser power density and irradiation time.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by the comprehensive in vitro and in vivo data showing that both STS26T and S462 tumors can be effectively treated with appropriate parameter optimization. The dose-response experiments (Figures 4-6) demonstrate that treatment efficacy can be modulated. However, the claim would be strengthened by more systematic optimization studies and clearer guidelines for parameter selection.

result: MPNSTs are aggressive sarcomas with dismal prognosis, affecting ~10% of NF1 patients. They are insensitive to traditional chemotherapy, lack effective targeted drugs, and have limited benefit from chemotherapy/radiotherapy. Extended resection with negative margins is key to improving prognosis but faces challenges including surgical difficulty and high recurrence risk.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C6-C8 establish the clinical context and unmet medical need. These are well-supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Mowery and Clayburgh, 2019; Widemann, 2009; Vitolo et al., 2019; van Noesel et al., 2019; Kroep et al., 2011; Widemann and Italiano, 2018). This background appropriately motivates the need for new therapeutic approaches.

result: While PTT at NIR-III has demonstrated potential in cancer theranostics, traditional PTAs (both inorganic and organic) have significant limitations. Inorganic PTAs have poor biodegradability, processability, and apparent cytotoxicity. Organic PTAs face challenges in optimizing photothermal conversion efficiency and stability. Poor target specificity and biocompatibility of PTAs hinder clinical translation of PTT.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C9-C10 accurately summarize established knowledge about PTT and PTA limitations, supported by appropriate citations. This provides strong rationale for the PTA-free approach investigated in this study. The characterization of PTA limitations is consistent with the literature.

result: NIR-III (1600-1870 nm) possesses advantages for MPNST treatment: higher penetration depth and lower optical scattering than NIR-I/II, better performance in high-collagen tissue, and demonstrated safety in various medical applications. MPNSTs are located on body surfaces and have significantly upregulated collagen expression, making them suitable targets for NIR-III treatment.
evaluation: Claims C11-C17 establish the scientific rationale for using NIR-III specifically for MPNSTs. These are well-supported by appropriate citations (Sordillo et al., 2017; Horton et al., 2013; Choi et al., 2016; Le Guellec et al., 2016; Karube et al., 2006; Shi et al., 2016b; Sakimoto et al., 2006; Adatto et al., 2017). The logical connection between MPNST characteristics (surface location, high collagen) and NIR-III properties is sound.

result: The NIR-III laser has a higher power safety limit than NIR-I/II lasers. Its photothermal conversion is attributed to thermal molecular movement of the irradiated object. The high collagen content of MPNSTs ensures efficiency of photothermal ablation, and photothermal effects could be more concentrated in MPNSTs than adjacent normal tissue. NIR-III laser would effectively induce photothermal ablation of MPNSTs due to their surface layout characteristics.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 combine established physical principles (C43) with logical inferences based on MPNST characteristics and NIR-III properties. C42 is supported by Figure 1c-d. C44 is a reasonable inference from the combination of high collagen in MPNSTs (C16) and NIR-III's preferential interaction with collagen (C15). C45-C46 are logical speculations that are subsequently validated by the experimental results. The mechanistic framework is sound.

result: ER stress occurs when pathological conditions (including high temperature) impede proper protein folding in the ER, leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins. Cells initiate the UPR to restore ER homeostasis. ATF4 and ATF6 contribute to stress relief by inducing ER chaperones and upregulating ERAD components. Misfolded proteins are targeted for ERAD and degraded via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
evaluation: Claims C62-C64, C66-C67 accurately describe established mechanisms of ER stress and UPR, appropriately supported by citations (Qi and Chen, 2019). This background knowledge is correctly applied to interpret the RNA-seq findings. The mechanistic framework is consistent with current understanding of ER stress biology.

result: The most significantly upregulated mRNAs in the ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis pathway include UBA3, UBE2E1, and HERC3.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by RNA-seq data analysis (Supplementary file 3). This finding is consistent with the enrichment of the ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis pathway (C37) and supports the overall mechanistic interpretation of ER stress response involving ERAD.

result: NIR-III PTT could be combined with surgery (preoperatively to reduce surgical scope/risk, or postoperatively at resection margins to reduce recurrence risk) for MPNST treatment. This PTA-free NIR-III PTT approach may be generalized for treatment of other benign and malignant skin and soft-tissue tumors.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70, C76 are explicitly labeled as speculation about potential clinical applications and broader generalization. While the preclinical data support the feasibility of these applications, no clinical studies or experiments in other tumor types are provided. These represent reasonable future directions but require validation.

result: This PTA-free PTT strategy possesses unique advantages for clinical application and patient prognosis improvement due to excellent biocompatibility and predominant photothermal conversion efficiency of NIR-III laser.
evaluation: Claim C75 is a summary conclusion supported by the overall experimental results demonstrating efficacy (C22-C30, C72-C74) and safety (C31, C59). The advantage of avoiding PTAs is logical given the established limitations of PTAs (C5, C9-C10). However, the claim of 'unique advantages' for clinical application is somewhat overstated without direct clinical data.

result: Two MPNST cell lines (STS26T from sporadic MPNST, S462 from NF1-MPNST) were used for in vitro experiments. The 1650 nm NIR-III laser system consisted of laser diodes, collimator lens, photodetector, spectroscope, focusing lenses, and optical fiber interface.
evaluation: Claims C47-C49 describe the experimental materials and methods. These are straightforward methodological descriptions supported by the text and Figure 2a. The use of two cell lines from different MPNST subtypes strengthens the generalizability of findings.
